title: Match a Simplified Regular Expression ('.' and '*')
statement:
A parser that validates a configuration string against a shape ("three
digits, a dash, then four digits") is doing regular-expression matching,
whether or not anyone calls it that or reaches for a library to do it. This
exercise builds the matcher itself, restricted to just enough syntax to
be genuinely awkward: a literal character, `.` for "any one character", and
`*` for "zero or more of whatever came immediately before it".

## Your function

```
bool regex_match(const char *s, const char *p);
```

Return `true` if pattern `p` matches the **entire** string `s` -- not a
substring, not a prefix, the whole thing. `s` contains only lowercase
letters. `p` contains lowercase letters, `.`, and `*`; it is always
well-formed, meaning `*` never appears as the first character of `p` and
never appears twice in a row -- every `*` has exactly one atom (a letter or
a `.`) immediately before it that it applies to.

## The recursive shape

Match `s` against `p` from the front. At each step, ask whether the pattern's
next atom matches the string's next character -- `p`'s next character equals
`s`'s next character, or `p`'s next character is `.` and `s` has a character
at all. Then:

- if the atom is **not** followed by `*` in the pattern, the atom must
  match, and both `s` and `p` advance by one atom;
- if the atom **is** followed by `*`, there are two ways forward that both
  have to be considered: skip the atom and its `*` entirely (zero
  repetitions), or, if the atom matched, consume one character of `s` and
  try the same pattern position again (one more repetition).

The base case: an empty pattern matches only an empty string.

## Watch out

- **`*` can legally match zero occurrences**, including of an atom that
  never appears anywhere in `s` at all. `regex_match("", "a*")` is `true`
  -- there is no `a` in `s`, and none is required, because `a*` is allowed
  to contribute nothing.
- **Matching is anchored to the whole string.** `regex_match("aa", "a")` is
  `false`, not true-because-it-matches-a-prefix -- a real regex engine's
  `search` finds `p` somewhere inside `s`; this function's contract is
  `fullmatch`, and the two are not the same question.
- **A `*` group can be skipped in the middle of a pattern, not only when
  it is the last thing in it.** `regex_match("aa", "ab*a")` is `true`:
  `b*` contributes zero `b`s, and the pattern still has an `a` on the far
  side of it to match the string's second character. A solution that only
  considers "skip the star group" as an option when it is at the end of
  the pattern gets this wrong.
- **Plain recursion without memoisation can retry the same
  `(s position, p position)` pair many times** when a pattern chains
  several `*` groups together, because "skip" and "consume one and stay"
  both recurse and their sub-problems overlap. It happens to be fast enough
  on inputs this size either way, but recognising the overlapping
  subproblem is what turns this from a brute-force search into the
  dynamic-programming problem it actually is -- worth doing properly rather
  than by accident.
